questions.question: Did Jesus come to set people free from sin, from the law, or both?
questions.shortAnswer: Jesus came to set captives free. Sin was the master. The law named the problem but could not cleanse it. His death is the gift that breaks both the wage of sin and the yoke of earning your way to God.
answer: You become a slave to whatever you obey. Jesus came to proclaim liberty to captives. Paul then said: if you try to get right with God by going back under the law, you treat Jesus' death as unnecessary.
Salvation is a gift. Receive Jesus. He takes sin off the throne. Then you live as a son, not a slave — following the Spirit, not managing sin as your focus.

verses.note: Jesus reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled in Him — liberty to the captives.
Everyone who practices sin is a slave to sin. If the Son sets you free, you are free indeed.
Not under law but under grace. You are a slave of the one you obey. The gift of God is eternal life.
The law was a guardian until Christ came.
For freedom Christ has set us free. Do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.
If righteousness were through the law, Christ died for no purpose.
Saved by grace through faith — the gift of God, not works.

questions.question: Are Bar-Jesus and Elymas the same person?
questions.shortAnswer: Same man in Acts 13. Two names from different roots. Bar-Jesus means son of Joshua. Elymas is a title for a sorcerer — not a translation of Jesus.
answer: Luke confronts one sorcerer with two names. Bar-Jesus is a Jewish patronymic: son of Joshua / Yeshua.
Elymas comes from a root meaning wise or learned. It functions like magos — sorcerer. Luke says ‘that is what his name means’ about Elymas, not about Bar-Jesus.
There is no linguistic bridge from Elymas to the Greek name Iēsous.

verses.note: Bar-Jesus, also called Elymas the sorcerer.

questions.question: Where did Moses already promise righteousness apart from the law?
questions.shortAnswer: Genesis 15:6. Abram believed God, and it was credited as righteousness — before the law and before circumcision. Grace was never Plan B.
answer: Romans 3:21 says this righteousness is testified by the Law and the Prophets. Paul’s flagship text from Moses is Abraham in Genesis 15, unpacked in Romans 4.

Genesis 12 and 22 promise blessing to the nations through Abraham’s seed — Paul calls that the gospel preached beforehand. Deuteronomy 30 says the word is near you; Paul quotes it in Romans 10 as the righteousness that is by faith.

Even the sacrificial system said covering comes by substitution, not personal merit. The law was not the original pattern. Trusting God was. For the Prophets, Paul’s go-to line is Habakkuk 2:4: the righteous will live by faith.

questions.question: If kindness makes a bitter person angrier, should I still be kind — and what does heaping coals on their head mean?
questions.shortAnswer: Kindness is a gift, not weakness. Give it. Do not throw your pearls to someone who will only grind them into slander. The coals verse is not revenge. It is good that can wake a conscience while you leave the result with God.
answer: Some people never had to practice kindness to keep their place. Force and position were enough. They call dominance boundaries. They may even call themselves kind. Kindness is not a show and it is not weakness. Jesus tied it to the greatest command: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself. When you give the gift, joy comes with it.

You cannot demand that a hard person become kind. You also do not have to keep handing them trust, access, and explanations they will twist. Be kind. Do not chase their approval. Do not argue with their story about you.

If your enemy is hungry, feed him. In doing this you heap burning coals on his head, and the Lord will reward you. Paul adds: do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good. The heat is conscience, not your revenge. If they repent, good. If they stay bitter, you still did not become them. Your joy comes from the Father, not from their change.

questions.question: Does the Bible tell me to work hard to prove I’m saved?
questions.shortAnswer: No. Philippians 2:12 says work out, not work for or work to prove. The gift is already yours. The working is the visible outworking of it.
answer: The NLT lands the sense: work hard to show the results of your salvation. The Greek means carry through to completion something you already have.
Verse 13 keeps the engine where it belongs: God is working in you, giving the desire and the power. Cooperation, not earning. Participation, not passivity.
‘Prove your salvation’ language usually comes from performance anxiety. Name that distortion. Fruit is evidence, not currency.

verses.note: Work out — for God works in you.
